content: HINT2, or Histidine Triad Nucleotide Binding Protein 2, is a mitochondrial protein encoded by the HINT2 gene located on chromosome 9 in humans. This protein functions as an AMP-lysine hydrolase and phosphoramidase and may play a role in tumor suppression. As a member of the histidine triad nucleotide-binding (Hint) protein family, which is a subfamily of the histidine triad (HIT) family, HINT2 contains a conserved histidine and HIT sequence motif (His-X-His-X-His-X-X). The last two histidines in this motif contribute to the formation of a catalytic triad. The protein encoded by the HINT2 gene is 163 amino acids long and forms a 17-kDa homodimer. Compared to other Hint family members, HINT2 shares 61% sequence homology with HINT1 and 28% sequence homology with HINT3. Notably, HINT2 has a 35-amino acid extension at its N-terminal, which corresponds to a predicted mitochondrial import signal. HINT2 belongs to the HIT superfamily and the Hint subfamily, which are characterized as nucleotide hydrolases and transferases that act on the alpha-phosphate of ribonucleotides. The Hint family is the most ancient within the HIT superfamily, and its members are highly conserved across eukaryotes and archaebacteria. Hint proteins, including HINT2, function as AMP-lysine hydrolases and phosphoramidases. In mammals, HINT2 is expressed in the liver, adrenal cortex, and pancreas, where it localizes to the mitochondria, specifically in the inner mitochondrial membrane facing the mitochondrial matrix. This positioning likely facilitates the transport of cholesterol from the cytosol to the mitochondrial matrix, a process essential for steroidogenesis. HINT2 may provide a contact site for the hydrophobic cholesterol molecule, enabling it to cross the mitochondrial intermembrane space. Additionally, HINT2 regulates steroidogenesis through calcium-dependent and calcium-independent signaling pathways, which may help maintain a favorable mitochondrial potential. Its role in calcium homeostasis may also contribute to its pro-apoptotic function in hepatocytes and other non-steroidogenic cells, although the exact mechanism remains unclear. Clinically, HINT2 is one of three members of the Hint protein family and is localized to the mitochondria of various cell types. In human adrenocarcinoma cells, HINT2 modulates mitochondrial calcium (Ca²⁺) handling. Intracellular calcium plays a critical role in numerous physiological processes across all living organisms. Extracellular stimuli generate temporally organized Ca²⁺ signals, often occurring as repetitive spikes. The frequency of these oscillations determines the nature and extent of the cellular response. These Ca²⁺ oscillations arise from the repetitive opening of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (InsP3) receptors, which are Ca²⁺ channels embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. The opening of these channels is initiated by a stimulus-induced rise in InsP3 levels. Because their activity is biphasically regulated by cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ levels, oscillations can occur. Mitochondria also influence cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ signals by buffering cytosolic Ca²⁺ changes and releasing Ca²⁺. At rest, the intramitochondrial and cytosolic Ca²⁺ concentrations are similar, approximately 100 nM. The Hint family, including HINT2, has been implicated in tumor suppression. HINT2, a member of the histidine triad protein superfamily, is exclusively localized to mitochondria, particularly near the contact sites of the inner membrane. This enzyme is highly expressed in the liver, where it has been shown to stimulate mitochondrial lipid metabolism, respiration, and glucose homeostasis. HINT2 modulates cytoplasmic and mitochondrial Ca²⁺ dynamics by enhancing the activity of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. The absence of HINT2 appears to lead to premature opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) in mitochondrial suspensions, which is associated with apoptosis and ischemia-reperfusion injury (e.g., during heart attacks) through calcium homeostasis. HINT2 is also observed to be upregulated in breast, pancreatic, and colon cancer cells, while it is downregulated in hepatocellular carcinoma and endometrial cancer. Although its exact role in tumor suppression remains unknown, studies suggest that HINT2 may promote apoptosis in hepatocellular carcinoma and endometrial cancer. In double knockout HINT2 mice, higher acylation and morphological alterations were observed in the mitochondria, suggesting that HINT2 may regulate glucose and lipid metabolism. Currently, no known protein-protein interaction partners have been identified for HINT2.
